hook_text: The most important history book in your home might be sitting on the couch.
clip_script: Apartheid ended just over thirty years ago. That means many people who lived under it are still with us. Grandparents. Neighbours. Teachers. They remember the pass book in the pocket. The bulldozers at the door. The sign on the beach that said who could swim there. Most of those stories were never written down, because the people who kept the records were the ones making the laws. Oral history changes that. You choose an apartheid law. You read about it. Then you sit down with someone it affected, ask permission, press record, and listen. Their memory becomes evidence. You check it against books, and you write it up. And a story that might have been lost becomes part of history.
visual_style: An elderly person speaking while a teenager listens with a phone recording; an old pass book; a black-and-white photo of a forced removal; a 'whites only' beach sign; a notebook with interview questions; a finished project with a bibliography.
pacing: Gentle and steady, with a pause before the interview begins.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how to plan your oral history project.
